notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0022.stoa013.opp-la: Printed page numbers (365, 367, 368), stray footnote letters and scanning errors (e.g. 'naturentur' for 'saturentur', 'dicit' for 'ducit', 'dut' for 'dux', 'commiti' for 'committi', 'obligavit' possibly for 'obrigavit') have been read as evident. Some scripture references in the edition are misprinted (e.g. '1 Petr.' for 2 Pet. 2:22) and are given corrected. In chapter II the text is damaged at 'in via I... et spatiosa'; 'lata' (broad), as in Matt. 7:13, is supplied. 'Initium vitae hominis spiritaliter arguetur' is attributed to Sirach 39:31 but does not match it; the sense is uncertain. 'Aliam carnem sequuntur' echoes Jude 7 ('going after other flesh').

Line 3: 'ora, mia' read as 'ora, filia' or similar; rendered 'my [daughter]'. 'Machabaeam' taken as the mother of the Maccabean martyrs. Ps. 140:4 citation reads 'Ptal. egL' in the scan. 'Sermones' in line 7 ('solos sermones ... Ambrosianos certo vocari') understood as sermons Ambrose himself reworked into books.

Line 11: the end is garbled in the scan ('uos cum C"i- biensinemini astruimus'); read as 'nos cum Corbeiensi Maximo astruimus', which is uncertain. Line 15: 'Laud male quadrat' read as 'haud male quadrat'. Line 20: 'Hos ... remiuere' read as 'nos ... remittere'. Line 24: 'hulc ant' read as 'huic tam'. Line 21: 'ladniis' read as 'laciniis' (digressions, patches).

Line 38 is badly garbled in the scan ('De in caput i Isaiæaliud quoque sentiendum est: sed nec etiam de sermonibus duobus in sermone Danielis; hi quippe non omnes... indicata caput XIII cujusque iuscriptione'). Translated as evidently intended: 'De [sermone] in caput I Isaiae [non] aliud... de sermonibus duobus in caput XIII Danielis; hi quippe omnes...' with 'caput XIII' displaced and 'non' misplaced. Line 35: 'feriodos' read as 'periodos', 'cixac' as 'CIX ac'.

nodes.text: TO A VIRGIN DEVOTED [TO GOD].

CHAPTER ONE. (Ps. 44:11, 12.) Hear, daughter, and see: incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house; for the King has desired your beauty; for he himself is the Lord your God, and they will worship him. You have vowed yourself to be his bride; you are called one devoted to God. What have you to do with worldly men, or what dealings do you have with them? What do you want to know in their company? The perdition which they themselves pursue? If you seek chastity, they do not have it; if you seek faith, who among them is faithful, that you should keep him company? But if you seek Christ, he does not abide in them. I do not know what you are seeking, what sort of friendships or what sort of talk you have with them. You vowed your soul to the destruction of all the things that belong to this world: how then do you seek the world which you renounced? You want to return to your vomit like a dog, or like a washed sow back to wallowing, as it is written (2 Pet. 2:22), and as the Apostle says: If I build up again the things I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor of the law (Gal. 2:18). Again he himself repeats, saying: Whatever is in the world is the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes (1 John 2:16): which is not of God, but is of this world. Likewise elsewhere he says: Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be made an enemy of God (James 4:4). What do you say, you who are devoted to God? Why do you want to please men? What do you desire, or what do you seek? If you seek God, he is with you; but if you seek a man, that is not what you vowed. What are men? Men of this world: And the world passes away, and its lust; but whoever does what is written abides for ever (1 John 2:17). What you desire, I do not know. If gold, silver, if wine, if splendid clothing, this has not pleased you in God's sight; God does not admire this, but a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. 50:19). Why do you seek the men of the world, whom the holy apostle Paul judges, saying: Whose god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things; but our citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3:19-20)? If then we have our citizenship in heaven, we ought to seek the things that are above, where Christ is, not the things upon the earth (Col. 3:1-2). I ask, sister, who are these men of this world? You do not follow your brothers, spiritual men, and you follow carnal ones, who, if they are not filled, will grumble. You have cast your pearls before swine, to trample them under their feet and turn and dash you down. Have you not heard: Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers (Phil. 3:2)? Who are these? Men of this world, who do not follow in the footsteps of Christ. I ask you, what do they show you? Tell me. Chastity, which they do not have? Why, faith, which they do not find? Teaching, which they do not follow, except the devilish wisdom of this world? Fasting, which they hate? Abstinence, which they condemn? Humility, which they crush? Sobriety, which they neglect? A sincere mind, which they do not have, only a double one? Modesty, which they cast away from themselves? I do not know what you want to pursue with them.

CHAPTER II. But what do you say? "I, however, am converting them to myself." But if they are converted to you, it does not profit you. What does the wolf seek with the lamb? Or what does a dog seek, except bread? And why does the lion roar (Isa. 31:4), except for prey? Keep yourself chaste, if you can. Why do you want to teach what you yourself do not do? As the Apostle says: Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God (1 John 4:1). But if you receive teaching from them, they will teach you what they do or what they pursue: lust, fornication, wantonness, avarice, fraud, uncleanness, shamelessness, luxury, drunkenness, wickedness, foul talk, folly, sorceries, murders, anger, strife and every malice. What do you say, wretched woman, or what excuse do you make? You vowed your soul so that you would withdraw from these very men: but now what are you seeking? I ask, are you not ashamed when they make up stories among themselves about you, saying: "Look, one devoted to God, who follows us; for she has abandoned her own way and wandered through the boundaries of her field, she has not found the way to her dwelling. Come, let us get hold of her first, and we will lead [her] into our way." You have fallen, wretched woman, onto the [broad] and spacious way that leads to death. That seems good to you which is evil: you follow them senselessly, and do not know that you are falling straight into a pit. Do you not remember that narrow and strait is the way that leads to life (Matt. 7:13-14)? That which is good seems laborious to you: have you forgotten that it was said: That through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of heaven (Acts 14:21)? But now you want to pursue your own will. Have you not read Solomon saying: For the good, good things were created from the beginning; likewise for the impious and sinners, good things and evil (Sir. 39:30)? Likewise he himself says: The beginning of a man's life will be reproved spiritually (ibid., 31). The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one (1 Cor. 2:15). Where are you, you devoted to God? The spiritual man indeed judges others, [yet] you yourself are judged. What do you seek with them? What part has the faithful with the unbeliever (2 Cor. 6:15)? Or what part has a holy person with the flesh? You may be a virgin in body, but corrupt in mind. Your eyes are blinded by an excessive heat of lust, in which a beam lies; your ears are full of every male filth; and your feet are swift, and not slow to go out of doors. Where is holiness? Where is modesty? Where is sobriety? Where is gravity? Where is chastity? Where is moderation? Where is faith? Where is continence? Where is a pure mind? Where are all those things for which you had pledged your faith, which you have lost? For it had been better for you not to vow and to do, than to vow and not to do (Eccl. 5:4). You cannot serve two masters, either God or mammon, as it is written (Matt. 6:24). With the perverse you will be perverted (Ps. 17:27). An old cloth cannot be joined to a new one; for it takes away its strength, and the tear becomes worse (Matt. 9:16). Birds gather to their own kind; and truth will return to those who practise it. Far be it that you should be called my sister, you who associate with such people. Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad. Every tree is known by its fruit (Matt. 12:33). Whoever a person may be, he joins himself to one like himself (Sir. 13:20). The dove sent out from the man's hand at once returned to him into the ark; but the raven sent out followed flesh (Gen. 8:7); and you too want to follow it, so as not to return to the door of Christ. Your company is with the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky: like the raven, you do not remember the Lord who freed you from the flood. You do not seek your shady and good resting-place, where you had rest for a time. The storm is not before your eyes, and you have forgotten the love of Christ, and you hold to the love of the men of this world, who have no love in them except a devilish one: they follow other flesh, and do not cease until they die. Withdraw, wretched woman, from those men, lest they devour your choice flesh, overthrow your children, and you be left naked and stripped, like [a hut] in a cucumber field. And now what will you do, since you are naked and stripped? You will go to your neighbours, whom you hated before, asking them for a covering for your shame: but they will not give it, saying: "Where is your splendid garment, which you used to wear before?" What do you say, and what do you answer, you whom the cold has gripped? They rejoice at the evils that have come upon you. Then you will lament yourself, saying: "Woe is me, wretched woman, to whom such things have come! What good did that captivity do me, which took me captive, wretched and unhappy? Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings before the dawn and dwell at the farthest part of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me" (Ps. 138:7 ff.). Then you will say: "I will go and return to my first husband, for it was better for me then than now (Hos. 2:7 ff.): he gave me my clothing, and my oil in its season. But now what shall I do?" Then you will return to your house weeping, from which you had gone out rejoicing. You will sit in a corner of your house mourning and saddened, weeping day and night, seeking someone to be saddened together with you, and there will be none; and those to console you, and you will not find them. And those whom you hated before will give you alms, and will shake their heads over you, saying: "Look, she who was devoted to God has now become like dung in the road, and like a city that is stormed. Where is her chastity? Where are all those things that used to attend her? They have abandoned her; for chastity was their leader: she lost chastity, and all those things fled." And now what will you do, wretched woman? Where are those whom you pursued? Let them redeem you, if they can. What exchange can you give for your soul, which you defrauded through your disobedience, in not listening to your brothers or sisters, who showed you that you should not join yourself to worldly men? But now what shall we do for you, or what shall we say, we whom you refused to hear, except to lament ourselves over you, saying: Spare, Lord, spare? May he perhaps deign to hear our weeping and groaning, so as to give you the will to turn to him anew, that you may recall your sins, saying: How many of my father's hired servants have bread in abundance, but I am perishing with hunger? I will rise, then, and go to my father, and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your daughter; receive me as one of your maidservants, that I may live (Luke 15:17 ff.). What if perhaps he kills that fatted calf for you? For I am jealous over you with jealousy; for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. For I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the love that is in Christ Jesus (2 Cor. 11:2 ff.).

CHAPTER III. — See, then, and beware of these men, so that you may be called my sister and lady. Enter into your chamber, and with the door shut pray to your Father (Matt. 6:6), that he may give you a good mind and understanding, so that you may know whom you ought to follow and whom to avoid; for there are many who feign to be what they are not, but they lie; and you do not know that it is your soul that is at stake; lest they lead you captive, like an ox that is led to the slaughter, or like a dog, to be tied up. Do not hasten like a bird into the snare. Listen to me: remove your foot from them, sit diligently in your house, work with your hands what is good, so that you may have something to share with those who suffer need. Pray without ceasing, and do not be seen readily in the streets. Fight the good fight, run more swiftly, so that you may lay hold of that for which you have been laid hold of by Christ (Phil. 3:12). Let men hear of you and rejoice in your good spirit and in the mind by which you live. Give alms, and behold, all things will be clean for you (Luke 11:41). Do not be reluctant to visit the sick, for by these you will be made firm in love. You shall not swear at all, neither by what is true nor by what is false; but let your speech be: Yes, yes; No, no; for whatever is more than this is from evil (Matt. 5:34 ff.). Be angry, and do not sin, by making excuses for sins with men who work iniquity (Ps. 140:4). Humble yourself, daughter, before the Lord, for God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5:5). Draw near to the Lord, that he may enlighten you, and you will not be ashamed in his sight (Ps. 33:6). Withdraw from the pleasure of the world and clothe yourself with the constancy of virtue. Lay aside the garments of this world and clothe yourself with the tunic of everlastingness. Abandon the foods of this world and take for yourself the holy of holies. Remember that Shadrach, Meshach, Abednego and Daniel refused the meat and wine of the gentiles and took for themselves vegetables and pulses (Dan. 1:8 ff.). Remember that the Maccabean woman suffered on account of pork, and that her sons were roasted or fried in oil (2 Macc. 7:1 ff.). Walk, daughter, in holy attire, with modesty and sobriety and gravity. Put away lying; speak the truth with your neighbour. Pray, my [daughter], without ceasing; fast often, and give alms; for almsgiving delivers from death and does not allow one to go into darkness (Tob. 4:11). Almsgiving is a good gift, which cleanses away all filth and squalor. You will be blessed if, when you have read all these things, you do them. Be zealous for what is good, so that you may forget what is evil. May the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit bless you with the blessing with which he deigned to bless our fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Pray for me, daughter, for I too am anxious for you, as it is written: Pray for one another (James 5:16). Likewise: A brother helping a brother will be exalted (Prov. 18:19). May the Lord exalt you in holiness and love, as it is written: He who loves his brother has fulfilled the Law (Rom. 13:8). May the Lord fulfil all your petitions (Ps. 19:7). May God the Father grant you this through Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord and God, king, judge, saviour and redeemer, who is blessed with the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.
NOTICE ON THE SERMONS HITHERTO PUBLISHED UNDER THE NAME OF AMBROSE.

Of the sermons which can be read through in the older editions of our Ambrose, almost no one has made mention who has not recognised that no small part of them is wrongly attributed to that holy man, and is circulated among the works of other Fathers, above all of blessed Maximus. The Roman edition, far from remedying this inconvenience, chose to add others besides, still more foreign to Ambrose's genius and style than those first ones. But this is not the only fault of that edition in this matter; for besides, it removed not a few sermons from the class of others and relegated them to places not their own, and on its own authority altered many things, both in the titles and in the text itself, so that they would seem more Ambrosian; whence it came about that men otherwise most shrewd were led into error.

Therefore, to free readers in future from deception of this kind, we resolved to bring to examination all the sermons which bear the name of Ambrose in any editions whatever. In this review, after applying diligence and rigour greater than which we could not, we found among those sermons — excepting four addresses, namely on the funeral of Valentinian, on the funeral of Theodosius, on not handing over the basilicas, and on the relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, which we have published in their proper places — not a single one which we judged could be attributed to Ambrose with any appearance or likeness of truth. For indeed everything there seemed to us so much at variance with the holy Doctor's diction and manner of treatment that we do not doubt that all who examine these same sermons with due attention will come over to our opinion.

As for Cassiodorus (On the Institution of Divine Letters, ch. 5) affirming that in his time there existed homilies or sermons bearing the name of Ambrose at their head, unless he is believed to have been deceived by his memory or by someone's false report, it must be said that those copies perished long ago. As for the manuscripts that contain the sermons now attributed to that bishop, we consider them of no authority. For for the most part they either show a more recent hand, or were books serving choral use, namely lectionaries and homiliaries, whose weight no one will deny is very slight. But not even in the older codices is it safe enough to put trust in this matter. For experience teaches that, to make them more saleable, great names were very often inscribed by copyists on the homilies or sermons of which they consisted. This very thing is plainly recognised in these sermons; for though we have no older copies of them than the Lyons codex, for whose variant readings we are indebted to the friendship of the most distinguished Baluze, and the St Gall codex, which our Mabillon, who handled and examined it, testifies was written a thousand years ago, nevertheless each of them contains sermons falsely displaying as author — the St Gall codex Augustine, the Lyons codex Ambrose — and for the most part to be restored to Saint Maximus, as Mabillon himself declares regarding the St Gall ones. From the verdict on these you may judge of the Lyons codex, since almost the same sermons are presented in both codices.

Nor will anyone be surprised that so many sermons are ascribed to blessed Maximus, since it is well known how great a preacher this saint was. That no small part of his sermons was transferred to Ambrose's name may have happened, besides the frauds of copyists already mentioned, also from this: that since he diligently studied the works of our holy Doctor and inserted large fragments excerpted word for word from them, especially from the Commentary on Luke, he gave careless scribes occasion to err. From this likewise it may perhaps be permissible to conjecture that no other author is to be sought for the books or sermons On the Sacraments than this same Maximus; a conjecture which place and time support.

What we have said so far makes plain that only those sermons can certainly be called Ambrosian which were put into the form of books by Ambrose himself, and of which almost the whole first volume is composed, and a large part of the second as well. We shall therefore not seem to have acted rashly in publishing none of those we examine here among the genuine and established works of the holy Doctor. And since some of these are extant in print only among Ambrose's works, while others are published elsewhere too, we shall present only the former, so that the volume may not grow with less useful bulk. However, to make it clearer that we have by no means used too free a judgement, we shall briefly set at the head of each sermon the reasons by which we were led not to consider it Ambrosian. Nor on that account shall we resist if any reader sets out to claim these same sermons for our Ambrose with stronger arguments.

As for those addresses which circulate in the works of other Fathers, since beyond the rest they also labour under the prejudice that they have been assigned no more to Ambrose than to Maximus or someone else, we have cut them out less timidly. But lest this change cause anyone trouble, provision will be made by a double index. In the first of these the omitted sermons will be arranged in such an order that one can see at a glance not only what place each formerly held in the Ambrosian editions, but also among which of the Fathers it is found. In the second index a threefold series of the sermons we retain will be set out so that all the Ambrosian editions, namely the old ones, the Roman, and our new one, may be compared side by side. But first some things pertaining specifically to the omitted sermons must be noted.

Sermons on the Seasons. — The first two, namely the first and third of the Roman edition, are attributed to Augustine in the St Gall codex, but in the Corbie and Saint-Germain codices, and in many others, they are given to Maximus, of whom they breathe entirely. The same may also be said of the following one, whose true title the Lyons codex gives as this: To be spoken before the Lord's Nativity.

The fourth of the omitted sermons, which is the sixth of the Roman edition, is assigned to Caesarius in the Augustinian Appendix. We do not object to this opinion, content indeed to have pointed out that there are comparisons in it which, since they are read in the sermons mentioned above, seem to indicate interpolation. The sermon omitted after these, that is, the twelfth of the said edition, the same Appendix likewise attributes to Caesarius; certainly no one who has read it will attribute it to Ambrose. Nor shall we argue otherwise about the following one, which you may also find in the appendix of Augustine's sermons. For since some manuscripts ascribe it to Ambrose, others to Augustine, we, with the Corbie [codex], assign it to Maximus.

The one that follows these begins in the oft-cited Appendix only with these words: The Lord says in the Gospel, etc. The St Gall codex likewise divides it so that the same words are the opening of a new sermon. How inept this division is can be recognised at first sight. This one, moreover, like the following, which seems to be its continuation, they assign with the best right to Maximus; but the one too which the Roman edition numbers twenty-fourth has long since been claimed for the same bishop.

Of the two following, the former was once placed fifty-sixth among the Augustinian sermons; now it has been restored to Caesarius, whose diction it closely resembles. The latter was returned with no less right to the same Father; yet no small part of it is inserted in a certain sermon of Rabanus, whose heading is: On the Fast of the Lord, and the reason for the Lenten Fast.

The thirty-ninth sermon of the Roman edition is titled thus: Why Christ [kept] fasts in the desert, etc. This is the hundred and forty-seventh in the Augustinian Appendix, and it and two others, namely the thirty-seventh and the thirtieth, of which one discusses the first temptation of Christ, the other the second, are by one and the same author, but most certainly not by Ambrose. For they are as far removed from his style as they come close to that of Maximus.

The one placed at number forty-one in the Roman edition, large fragments of which are found in Rabanus Maurus's homily for the third Sunday of Lent, is assigned in the Augustinian Appendix to Saint Caesarius. Yet there fits this sermon not badly what Gennadius records, that Maximus wrote addresses On the special Fast of Lent, and that one must not jest during it. But on other grounds it seems no less to be Caesarius's than the twenty-sixth sermon of the Roman edition, which no one doubts was written by him.

The forty-second of the said edition has absolutely nothing that does not savour of Saint Maximus. The same must likewise be decided about the forty-seventh, whose beginning the same Roman edition had wrongly altered, and which Gennadius indicates is owed to Maximus under this title: On Judas the Traitor.

To these let the forty-eighth be added, and those that depend on it, the forty-ninth and the fiftieth. For everything proclaims that these are Maximus's. We cannot, however, refrain here from remonstrating with the Roman editors, who, both elsewhere and in the last of these sermons, did not hesitate to change a great many things against the other editions and manuscripts.

The fifty-first sermon, like the two placed immediately after it, is also found among those of Maximus. Nor do we doubt that these are the very ones recorded by Gennadius under these titles: On the Cross of the Lord, On his Sepulchre, On his Resurrection. Likewise of the same Maximus are the fifty-fifth and the fifty-sixth, which is a continuation of the fifty-third, just as the fifty-seventh is of the fifty-fifth.

The fifty-eighth is restored to Caesarius in the Augustinian Appendix, and it has absolutely nothing to explain why it was once attributed to Ambrose. Nor did the sixtieth deserve with better right to be reckoned under his name. For besides being claimed for Maximus in his editions and in not a few manuscripts, what is said in it about the baptism of the Apostles plainly conflicts with what may be read in the Apology of David, chapter 9, number 50.

Besides other things, this too claims the sixty-first for Maximus, that it seems to refer us to the fifty-seventh sermon, which we said above belongs to the same bishop. But what is mentioned here about the fast on the Saturday before Pentecost does not agree with what was taught on the same matter in the sixtieth; and therefore some doubt may arise whether it should perhaps be referred to an author later than the same Maximus.

The sixty-fourth sermon is nothing other than Basil's homily on that saying from the Gospel according to Luke: I will pull down my barns, etc., though with some things partly added, partly cut away. We have seen that Ambrose used the same Basilian homily in the book On Naboth; yet one may not infer from this that Ambrose is also the author of this sermon. On the contrary, if what Saint Ambrose imitated from that homily in that same book is compared with this sermon, it will at once be recognised that our Doctor rendered Basil's thoughts in a far nobler manner than the translator of this sermon; for he, rendering word for word slavishly, in his whole style, and especially in the digressions which he wove in of his own from time to time, is as far as possible from Ambrose.

The sixty-sixth, which stands at the same number in the Appendix of Augustinian sermons, Mabillon thinks can be connected with the eleventh, which he published as Maximus's. Yet its style, in our judgement at least, differs so much from this Father's manner of writing that we would more willingly assign the same sermon to some later author.

In the Roman edition some addresses had been placed after the Sermons on the Seasons, of which the first three, namely on the Basilicas, and at the funeral of the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius, we have presented each in its own place; the fourth, however, we wished to leave to Maximus alone, whose style it savours of and whose name it already bears in the Library of the Fathers.

Sermons on the Saints. — The second of the sermons called On the Saints was published among both Augustine and Maximus; but not only its diction but also its affinity with the fifty-eighth claims it for the latter.

The fifth sermon, which was delivered by Ambrose on the brother martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, we have placed among the letters; that this is its genuine place was shown in the Preface set before them.
The sixth sermon was long ago returned to Maximus, and it is not obscure that it was spoken by none other than the bishop of Turin.

The tenth is said in the Appendix to Augustine's Works to be attributed perhaps more truly to Ambrose than to Augustine; but to us it seems truly to be denied to both, and with equal right. For if you weigh its diction, you will readily admit that it is no more Ambrose's than Augustine's; and at the same time you will notice that its author seems to be later than Chrysostom.

The twelfth you may also find in the Augustinian Appendix, but besides it exists among the works of Maximus, to whom it is also attributed by consensus of scholars. Nor should anything else be decided about the thirteenth, since it is a continuation of the twenty-fourth sermon on the Seasons, which we saw above is Maximus's.

To the seventeenth a certain fragment is prefixed in the Roman edition which is omitted in the old ones; the same Augustinian Appendix presents this sermon complete. And to make it plain that there is nothing Ambrosian in that sermon, let it simply be compared with what Ambrose wrote about Saint Lawrence in the books of Duties.
The eighteenth is read among the sermons of Maximus, and his genius and style are detected in it.

The twentieth too is to be found among Maximus's works. If, however, it is to be ascribed to him, as it seems, it must have been titled On Saint Michael by some half-learned person for this reason, that on this feast the gospel which is the subject of this sermon was customarily read. Among the works of the same bishop of Turin the twenty-first exists with its true title, namely On Hospitality; and so it is credible that this is the very one which Gennadius attests was written by the same bishop On Avarice and Hospitality. The Roman edition therefore had no reason to title it On the Feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist.

Sermons from the earlier volumes. — The sermon On the Forbidden Tree heads the order in Augustine's Appendix. It is observed there that this sermon has variant readings among Ambrose's works, but these were introduced by editors for the sake either of elegance or of greater kinship with Ambrose's style. It is no wonder, then, if someone even of more learned judgement, deceived by these, thought nothing prevented the same sermon from being attributed to the holy Doctor. Its author is wholly unknown. Manichaeans are indeed attacked there, but not strict ones, since these do not deny that wine is good. Therefore they must have been either Marcionites or those heretics whom Ambrose refutes in the book On Paradise, where the same subject is treated, but in a far different way.

Our Mabillon had the two sermons On Saint Elisha published in the first part of the Museum Italicum as though they had not yet been made public; but the cause of the error must be traced to the confusion of the Roman edition, where they had been placed out of their proper position. For the rest, we shall by no means object to their being called Maximus's.

The genuine title of the sermon on chapter 7 of Job is this: On not fearing carnal enemies; and on giving thanks after food. For by this title Gennadius identifies it, and he also indicates that it is by Maximus, among whose works it is likewise found.

The expositions or sermons on Psalms 21, 109 and 117 may rightly be counted among Maximus's. In the Ambrosian editions the first of these sermons presents certain passages which are not found among Maximus's works, but these are not of great importance. The third, moreover, has been restored to the same Maximus in the Roman breviary.

The exposition on chapter 31 of Proverbs can be read in its pure form among the works of Augustine, to whom it is ascribed, and without those additions which the Roman edition wove into it so that it would be judged more Ambrosian.
The two sermons On Almsgiving on chapter 3 of Ecclesiasticus are attributed to Saint Maximus, whose diction they reproduce beautifully, in his editions as well.

Nor is anything else to be thought about [the sermon] on chapter 1 of Isaiah, nor yet about the two sermons on chapter 13 of Daniel; for all of these are both found among Maximus's works and asserted by Gennadius to be his, the title of each being indicated.

The first of the sermons on chapters 3 and 4 of Jonah belongs to no one but Maximus, to whom the editions of that same Father, as well as Gennadius, assign it; the second was published by Mabillon in the Museum Italicum under Maximus's name. That he thought it not yet published must be blamed on the disorder of the Roman edition.
Finally, since the sermon on chapter 1 of Malachi is a continuation of the sermon on chapter 7 of Job, which we proved above to be Maximus's, it is clear that it also belongs to the same author.
